title: Yes, they can: Developing transcription skills and oral language in tandem with SRSD instruction on close reading of science text to write informative essays at grades 1 and 2
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a longstanding debate in early literacy instruction: whether students in the primary grades should first master foundational transcription and oral language skills before being taught higher-level composing processes, or whether these can be developed simultaneously. The study also examines whether first- and second-grade students can learn to do close reading of informational science texts and then use those texts to plan and write informative essays—an area the authors note is rarely emphasized in early elementary classrooms despite standards expectations.

The intervention studied was “SRSD Plus,” a multicomponent instructional approach that combines Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) for close reading, planning, and informative writing with explicit instruction in transcription and oral language. The “Plus” elements included handwriting fluency, spelling, vocabulary, and sentence proficiency; the SRSD component emphasized strategy instruction, self-regulation, discussion, modeling, planning, and genre knowledge for writing informative essays from source texts. Students in the treatment condition received teacher-led instruction in small groups for 45 minutes, three times per week, over 10 weeks, while comparison students received business-as-usual writing instruction described by teachers as writers workshop. Teachers delivering SRSD Plus received practice-based professional development and ongoing implementation support.

The study was conducted in one high-poverty elementary school in the southeastern United States with 93 first- and second-grade students, who were randomly assigned within class to SRSD Plus or business-as-usual. Outcomes included writing quality, planning, structural elements of informative essays, use of source text, transition words, number of words written, spelling, handwriting fluency, vocabulary, sentence proficiency, and discourse knowledge. Assessments were administered before and immediately after the intervention, and treatment fidelity was monitored through structured observations.

The main conclusion is that young students can successfully develop transcription skills, oral language, and composing abilities at the same time. Compared with business-as-usual writers workshop, SRSD Plus produced moderate to large positive effects on writing outcomes, oral language skills, spelling, and discourse knowledge, with especially strong gains in writing quality and planning. The findings support integrated, explicit, evidence-based literacy instruction in the early grades rather than delaying composition instruction until foundational skills are fully developed.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial with student-level random assignment, blinded assessors, fidelity data, and a clearly defined business-as-usual comparison in a relevant K-2 literacy context. Although some comparator implementation details were missing, the design meets the standard for a strong RCT with high relevance to K-12 literacy instruction.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced medium-to-large effects on multiple literacy outcomes, including writing quality (g=1.02), planning (g=1.40), and other writing measures, in a high-poverty early elementary population. These effect sizes indicate substantial educational impact relative to business-as-usual writers workshop.

finding.finding_summary: This randomized controlled trial compared teacher-led SRSD Plus with business-as-usual writers workshop for Grade 1-2 students (n=93; posttest n=90) in a high-poverty school. SRSD Plus produced statistically significant improvements across writing-related literacy outcomes, including writing quality (effect size g=1.02), planning (g=1.40), structural elements in informative essays (g=0.29), use of source text (g=0.48), number of words written (g=0.82 in Grade 1; g=1.39 in Grade 2), and transition words (g=1.33 in Grade 1; g=2.46 in Grade 2). The intervention also improved spelling and discourse knowledge, supporting stronger early literacy composition performance than business-as-usual writing workshop.
finding.measure: Timed source-based informative essay writing tasks; writing quality rubric; planning rubric; structural elements rubric; number of words written; transition words; use of source text; spelling dictation; discourse knowledge interview
finding.effect_size: g=1.02 (writing quality); g=1.40 (planning); g=0.29 (structural elements); g=0.48 (use of source text); g=0.82 to 1.39 (number of words); g=1.33 to 2.46 (transition words)
finding.std_deviation: Sample mean age SD=0.48; outcome SDs not_reported

finding.finding_summary: SRSD Plus improved oral-language-related outcomes relative to business-as-usual writers workshop in this Grade 1-2 RCT (n=93). The abstract and methods/results summary report moderate to large positive effects for vocabulary and sentence proficiency, indicating that integrating oral language instruction with writing strategy instruction benefited early language development alongside writing.
finding.measure: Researcher-developed proximal vocabulary task and sentence proficiency task
finding.effect_size: moderate to large effect sizes reported, exact values not_reported in provided text
finding.std_deviation: Sample mean age SD=0.48; outcome SDs not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The intervention embedded close reading of science texts aligned to NGSS and asked students to write informative essays from science-related source texts, so science-content learning was part of the instructional context. However, the study did not report a standalone science reasoning or science achievement outcome; instead, science text comprehension was inferred through planning and use of source text, making evidence for scientific reasoning indirect rather than definitive.
finding.measure: Indirect indicators through comprehension/use of science informational source texts in planning and writing

finding.finding_summary: The study's theoretical framing emphasized self-regulation, motivation, persistence, and self-efficacy as targets of SRSD instruction, and fidelity observations suggested strong student responsiveness and engagement during implementation. However, no direct student-reported or validated social-emotional outcome measure was reported in the provided text, so the evidence is supportive but indirect.
finding.measure: Instructional fidelity ratings of student responsiveness/engagement; self-regulation emphasized in intervention design
